_note: kind: cultural, folk, seasonal, civic, religious. Religious and indigenous entries are acknowledged with respect; the daemon never role-plays deities or invents ceremonies for living religions.

festivals.name: New Year
festivals.explain: The calendar turns. Almost every culture marks a new year as a threshold: a time to close and to begin.
festivals.ritual: Write one thing to leave behind and one to carry forward.

festivals.name: Old New Year
festivals.explain: New Year by the old Julian calendar, still celebrated in Russia as a second, quieter New Year.
festivals.ritual: A small second chance: revisit the wish you made on 1 January.

festivals.name: Svyatki
festivals.explain: The twelve days from Orthodox Christmas to Epiphany: in Slavic folk tradition the classic season for fortune-telling (святочные гадания), with mirrors, candles and wax.
festivals.ritual: The traditional season for readings: a three-card spread each evening.

festivals.name: Three Kings' Day
festivals.explain: Families share the rosca de reyes; whoever finds the hidden figure hosts the next gathering on 2 February.
festivals.ritual: A day for small gifts and for noticing what came to you unexpectedly.

festivals.name: Candlemas
festivals.explain: Christian feast of light; in Mexico, whoever found the figure in the rosca serves tamales; in Puno, Peru, one of the largest festivals of the Andes.
festivals.ritual: Mention it respectfully; suggest lighting a candle for clarity, nothing more.

festivals.name: Festival of Iemanjá
festivals.explain: In Salvador and along Brazil's coast, crowds bring flowers to the sea for Iemanjá, the orixá of the sea in Afro-Brazilian religions.
festivals.ritual: A living religion: acknowledge it with respect, never role-play it or invent rituals for it.

festivals.name: International Women's Day
festivals.explain: A day of rights and recognition; in Russia a major public holiday with flowers.
festivals.ritual: Thank a woman who shaped you.

festivals.name: St John's Eve and Festa Junina
festivals.explain: Midsummer night in the north, the heart of winter in the south: bonfires, Brazil's Festa Junina (São João), Inti Raymi in Cusco on 24 June.
festivals.ritual: A fire ritual: write what you release and (safely) burn it.

festivals.name: Ivan Kupala
festivals.explain: Slavic midsummer night: wreaths floated on rivers, jumping over fires, searching for the fern flower that blooms only this night.
festivals.ritual: Float a wish on water, or write it on a leaf.

festivals.name: Day of the Pachamama
festivals.explain: Andean offering to Mother Earth through August; an indigenous practice that is alive today.
festivals.ritual: Acknowledge it with respect; suggest gratitude to the earth, not imitation of the ceremony.

festivals.name: Halloween
festivals.explain: The night before All Saints, descended from Samhain: the veil between worlds was said to be thin.
festivals.ritual: An ancestors spread.

festivals.name: Day of the Dead
festivals.explain: 1 and 2 November: families build altars (ofrendas) with cempasúchil marigolds, photos, food and candles to welcome their dead.
festivals.ritual: Name someone you miss and what they gave you.

festivals.name: All Souls' Day
festivals.explain: Families visit cemeteries to remember their dead.
festivals.ritual: A quiet ancestors spread, if the user wants it.

festivals.name: Our Lady of Guadalupe
festivals.explain: Mexico's largest religious celebration; millions walk to the Basilica.
festivals.ritual: Mention it with respect only.

festivals.name: Christmas
festivals.explain: Christmas; for many, a family celebration more than a religious one.
festivals.ritual: A gentle day; a reading only if asked.

festivals.name: Orthodox Christmas
festivals.explain: Christmas by the Julian calendar.
festivals.ritual: Mention it with respect only.

festivals.name: New Year's Eve
festivals.explain: Brazil's Réveillon: white clothes and jumping seven waves; in Latin America, twelve grapes at midnight, one wish each.
festivals.ritual: Twelve wishes, or a one-card reading for each coming month.

festivals.name: Carnival
festivals.explain: The days before Lent: Brazil's Carnival, Barranquilla's in Colombia. Masks and excess before restraint.
festivals.ritual: A playful reading: which mask are you wearing, and which would you like to try?

festivals.name: Holy Week
festivals.explain: The week before Easter, Palm Sunday to Easter Sunday.
festivals.ritual: Mention it with respect only.

festivals.name: Maslenitsa
festivals.explain: Butter week before Orthodox Lent: blini (round and golden like the sun) and the burning of a straw Maslenitsa figure to say goodbye to winter.
festivals.ritual: Name what you're ready to let winter take away.

festivals.name: Lunar New Year
festivals.explain: The new moon that begins the Chinese lunisolar year, celebrated around the world.
festivals.ritual: A new-moon intention, doubled.

festivals.name: Spring equinox (Ostara)
festivals.explain: Day and night are equal; the sun crosses the equator.
festivals.ritual: Balance: what is in balance, what is not?

festivals.name: Beltane (astronomical)
festivals.explain: Halfway between equinox and solstice. The traditional dates (1 May, 31 October) come a few days earlier.
festivals.ritual: In the north, fertility and fire; in the south, ancestors.

festivals.name: Summer solstice (Litha)
festivals.explain: The sun stands still at its northern turning point: longest day in the north, longest night in the south. In the Andes, Willkakuti, the Aymara New Year, greets the returning sun.
festivals.ritual: Light and dark: a solstice spread.

festivals.name: Lammas (astronomical)
festivals.explain: Halfway between solstice and equinox: first harvest in the north, first stirrings of spring in the south.
festivals.ritual: What are you harvesting, or what is stirring?

festivals.name: Autumn equinox (Mabon)
festivals.explain: Day and night are equal again.
festivals.ritual: Balance and gratitude.

festivals.name: Samhain (astronomical)
festivals.explain: Halfway between equinox and solstice; the traditional dates (31 October, 1 May) come a few days earlier.
festivals.ritual: In the north, ancestors; in the south, fire and growth.

festivals.name: Winter solstice (Yule)
festivals.explain: The sun's southern turning point: longest night in the north, longest day in the south.
festivals.ritual: Light and dark: a solstice spread.

festivals.name: Imbolc (astronomical)
festivals.explain: Halfway between solstice and equinox.
festivals.ritual: First light, or first harvest.

festivals.name: La Calabiuza
festivals.explain: On the night of 1 November in Tonacatepeque, La Calabiuza fills the streets with the figures of Salvadoran folklore: la Siguanaba, el Cipitío, el Cadejo, la Carreta Chillona.
festivals.ritual: Tell a ghost story from your family.

festivals.name: Day of the Dead (El Salvador)
festivals.explain: In El Salvador families visit the cemetery, clean and dress the graves with flowers and wreaths, and gather for a meal together; ayote en miel (pumpkin in honey) is a classic sweet of the season.
festivals.ritual: Share a meal, or set a plate for someone you miss.

festivals.name: Day of the Cross (El Salvador)
festivals.explain: Wooden crosses in patios are dressed with fruit and paper chains, a custom tied to the start of the rainy season.
festivals.ritual: Mention it with respect; the fruit is the season's gratitude.

festivals.name: Unity Day
festivals.explain: A Russian public holiday.
festivals.ritual: A day off; nothing more.
